newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis says confident in French deficit outlook.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis says confident in French deficit outlook.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Friday he had confidence in the government's growth, public deficit and social security deficits forecasts.
"I'd like to say to you, and repeat to you, that public spending is under control and the government will meet the 3 percent target...and 2.8 percent in 1998," Arthuis said at a news conference.
He said the public deficit figures for March showed an improvement so far in 1997 compared with 1996.
"The first elements we have for March point to an improvement of around 18 billion (francs) over last year," Arthuis said.
Arthuis also said the government would take any necessary measures to prevent the social security deficit from overshooting the government's 1997 target.
"I have no reason to worry. If there were slippage at any moment, we would take sufficient measures," he said.
Arthuis repeated that he was confident of 2.3 percent growth in gross domestic product in 1997 and 2.8 percent growth in 1998, in line with official forecasts.

Amid press speculation that value added tax (VAT) receipts were weakening, Arthuis told reporters that procedures introduced last year for speeding up reimbursements to companies had had a one-off effect.
He said it was normal that the pattern of VAT receipts would then even out over the year.
Concern that France could miss 1997 public deficit targets outlined in the Maastricht Treaty to allow it join a single European currency in 1999 have been growing this week.

The catalyst was a press report in French daily Le Monde which said the budget division of the finance ministry had produced a confidental "forecast note" which said the 1997 deficit could hit 3.5 percent of GDP, taking account of the cutbacks planned so far.
Part of the "worst scenario" calculation for this year was a social security deficit of 47 billion francs, 17 more than planned, the paper said.

Arthuis issued a statement late on Thursday to quell the speculation, which was weighing on bond markets, in which he said the government would take any steps necessary to ensure the three percent target was met.
